July 28, 2024 
 
To Whom it May Concern; 
 
I am writing to comment on the EPA’s proposed regulation for N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP) as a 
laboratory chemical under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) (Docket ID EPA–HQ–
OPPT–2020–0744). While I appreciate the EPA’s efforts to protect public health and close 
existing regulatory gaps, I believe the proposed rule is poorly tailored to the unique nature of 
laboratory operations and creates an unnecessary regulatory burden. 
EPA should align its requirements for laboratory use of hazardous chemicals, including NMP, 
more closely with OSHA’s Laboratory Standard. EPA should develop a common regulatory 
approach to mitigating the risks of chemical exposures in laboratories, and apply that approach 
to all chemicals for which EPA is currently proposing to regulate, or may regulate in the future, 
under TSCA. 
Shortcomings of Existing Regulation 
To date, the use of hazardous chemicals in laboratories has been regulated primarily by OSHA’s 
Laboratory Standard (29 CFR 1910.1450). This represents a significant improvement for 
laboratories over previous OSHA regulations including the Hazard Communication Standard and 
substance-specific regulations in 29 CFR 1910 Subpart Z. However, while the Laboratory 
Standard has been beneficial, OSHA’s regulations fail to protect non-employees (e.g. students 
working in academic labs) and many public-sector employees. This is a notable gap that EPA 
can, should, and has begun to address in recent rulemakings under TSCA. It is crucial that any 
changes in the final rule maintain this advantage over the existing OSHA regulation. This will 
ensure a more comprehensive and up-to-date approach to safety in laboratories, benefiting all 
who work within them. 
Common Approach to Chemical Regulation Aligned with OSHA Standards 
EPA should develop a common approach to mitigating the risks of chemical exposures in 
laboratories and apply this approach to all chemicals regulated under TSCA. This would reduce 
the compliance burden on laboratories, which use hundreds to thousands of chemicals. A single, 
holistic Chemical Hygiene Plan would be more effective than a multitude of chemical-specific 
compliance programs. 
A unified approach would not only streamline compliance but also enhance safety by providing a 
consistent framework for managing chemical risks. Laboratories are dynamic environments 
where the introduction of new chemicals and procedures is routine. A common regulatory 
approach would allow laboratories to adapt more swiftly and effectively to new regulations, 
ensuring that safety measures are always up-to-date and comprehensive. Aligning with OSHA’s 
Laboratory Standard (29 CFR 1910.1450) would ensure that the regulations are practical and 
relevant to the actual conditions in which NMP is used in laboratories. 
EPA should develop a common approach to mitigating the risks of chemical exposures in 
laboratories and apply this approach to all chemicals regulated under TSCA. 

WCPP Framework 
The current proposed rule requires a Workplace Chemical Protection Plan (WCPP) that includes 
Direct Dermal Contact Controls for NMP. While this appears to offer flexibility, the requirements 
for the WCPP are not well-suited to laboratory operations. Laboratories use NMP in a wide variety 
of operations, often in small quantities and under conditions that differ significantly from industrial 
uses. 
Laboratories frequently handle NMP in volumes ranging from 0.1 to 500 mL. The chemical is 
typically both stored and used inside of containers, and is transferred between containers using 
syringes, cannulas, or funnels. The containers themselves are maintained within controlled 
environments such as fume hoods or glove boxes. These methods and settings inherently 
minimize the risk of direct dermal contact. This stands in stark contrast to industrial applications 
where NMP might be used in larger quantities, in more open environments, and in applications 
such as coatings or adhesive removers that increase risk of direct dermal contact. In other 
industrial settings such as manufacturing the use of NMP might involve continuous processes 
that are highly engineered and are performed consistently for many years. 
The WCPP framework is identical for industries with well-defined, consistent operations and for 
laboratories with diverse, variable operations. This one-size-fits-all approach is inappropriate for 
laboratories, which may only perform specific operations once and handle NMP exclusively in 
containers, making direct dermal contact unlikely. Clarifying the definition of direct dermal contact 
in the context of laboratory operations would help ensure that the regulations are appropriately 
targeted and do not impose unnecessary burdens on laboratory personnel. 
EPA should adopt a Laboratory Standard under TSCA that requires development of a 
single, holistic Workplace Chemical Protection Plan rather than require development of a 
multitude of distinct chemical-specific Workplace Chemical Protection Plans. 
Direct Dermal Contact Controls and PPE Selection 
The proposed rule requires that PPE used to provide dermal protection against NMP be “selected 
based on specifications from the manufacturer or supplier” and that such data establish that the 
PPE is “impervious to NMP alone, NMP-containing formulations, and in likely combination with 
other chemical substances in the work area.” This requirement would be difficult for operators of 
laboratories to satisfy given that existing test methodologies focus on protection against 
immersion or other forms of continuous contact. Such testing lacks relevance to laboratory work 
which requires protection against incidental or splash contact. 
Furthermore, the likely combinations of chemicals that laboratory workers may be reasonably 
expected to be exposed to when working with NMP are functionally infinite. The scope of the 
Laboratory Standard is defined in part by the use of multiple chemicals or chemical procedures. 
Most of these combinations will not have been envisioned by glove manufacturers, and, therefore, 
will not have been tested. 
PPE selection requirements should allow for reliance on the professional judgment of 
Chemical Hygiene Officers (CHO) and Certified Industrial Hygienists (CIH) when selecting 
PPE. 

Recordkeeping Requirements 
The recordkeeping requirements for PPE selection and usage in the proposed rule also do not 
align well with OSHA’s Laboratory Standard, Personal Protective Equipment Standard (29 CFR 
1910 Subpart I), or with how university laboratories are staffed. The Laboratory Standard requires 
that laboratories document “criteria that the employer will use to determine and implement control 
measures to reduce employee exposure to hazardous chemicals including engineering controls, 
the use of personal protective equipment and hygiene practices” within a Chemical Hygiene Plan 
(§1910.1450(e)(3)(ii)). OSHA’s PPE Standard, which also applies to laboratories that use 
hazardous chemicals, requires employers to “verify that the required workplace hazard 
assessment has been performed through a written certification that identifies the workplace 
evaluated; the person certifying that the evaluation has been performed; the date(s) of the hazard 
assessment; and, which identifies the document as a certification of hazard assessment” 
(§1910.132(d)(2)). 
EPA also proposes to require documentation of worker information that far exceeds that 
necessary to identify individual workers; specifically, “the name, workplace address, work shift, 
job classification, and work area of each person.” University laboratories in particular will struggle 
to collect this information. Persons who may handle NMP in university laboratories may be 
volunteers, visiting scholars, undergraduate students enrolled in laboratory courses, 
undergraduate students working as paid laboratory assistants, graduate students enrolled in 
laboratory courses, graduate students working as teaching assistants, graduate students working 
as paid laboratory researchers, graduate students receiving extramural fellowships, postdoctoral 
scholars, staff researchers, adjunct faculty, or tenured or tenure-track faculty. Each of those would 
represent a different job classification, and many researchers switch between classifications each 
academic period based on considerations that do not meaningfully impact the likelihood of 
exposure to NMP (e.g. a graduate student who had been working as a paid researcher receiving 
an extramural fellowship). Further complicating the issue of job classification within university 
laboratories is that universities commonly maintain information regarding students and employees 
within separate databases. 
Given the obstacles to satisfying the recordkeeping requirements including testing data, individual 
assignments, and demographic data contained the proposed rule, it could act as a de facto 
prohibition on the use of NMP in university laboratories. Aligning recordkeeping requirements with 
OSHA’s PPE Standard would ensure that laboratories can maintain effective safety practices 
without being overwhelmed by paperwork. 
EPA should replace the current proposed recordkeeping requirements with language 
identical to OSHA’s Laboratory Standard and PPE Standard, except as necessary to 
account for the applicability of the proposed rule to non-employees. 
Use of the Hierarchy of Controls 
The hierarchy of controls is a useful framework for structuring assessments of risk mitigations. 
However, documenting its use in each operation is not useful. As highlighted previously, 
laboratories are dynamic environments which frequently introduce new chemicals, and may only 
perform a specific operation a single time. While it may be sensible to document the rationale for 
eschewing elimination or substitution of NMP in a manufacturing plant, to do so for every operation 
performed in a laboratory simply generates excessive paperwork. 

Examples of controls provided in EPA’s discussion of its proposal to require incorporation of the 
hierarchy of controls illustrate the illogic of its formal application to laboratory use of NMP. 
Automation, enclosed transfer liquid lines with built-in purging mechanisms, closed-loop container 
systems, pneumatic tools, and tongs are irrelevant or impractical when handling small volumes in 
highly variable operations. In laboratory settings, engineering controls such as fume hoods and 
glove boxes are typically sufficient to manage exposure risks. The proposed reliance on more 
complex and industrial-scale controls is not practical for the small-scale, varied operations typical 
of laboratories. Allowing laboratories to use appropriate engineering controls based on the 
specific risks and conditions of their operations would be more effective and less burdensome. 
Any requirement to incorporate the hierarchy of controls should clarify that operators of 
laboratories will be permitted to satisfy such requirement by incorporating general 
provisions that apply across all operations into their existing documentation (e.g. a 
Chemical Hygiene Plan). 
Restricted Areas and Warning Signs 
EPA has requested comment on designation of “restricted areas” and on warning signage for the 
same. OSHA’s General Industry Standard for Beryllium (29 CFR 1910.1024(m)(2)) is offered as 
a potential model for these requirements. 
EPA should carefully consider the current and future scope of rulemaking under TSCA, and how 
those rules will apply cumulatively to laboratories when crafting any such requirements. In a 
typical laboratory, the entire lab room would typically be considered the regulated area. Numerous 
chemicals are used in various experiments, and the set of chemicals in simultaneous use changes 
daily. A typical academic organic chemistry laboratory can keep between 2000 and 5000 unique 
chemicals on hand. It is entirely foreseeable, therefore, that a single laboratory could be a 
regulated area for NMP, 1-bromopropane, 1,1-dichloroethane, 1,1,2-trichloroethane, 1,2-
dichloroethane, 1,2-dichloroethylene, 1,2-dichloropropane, 1,3-butadiene, 1,4-dioxane, multiple 
phthalates, acetaldehyde, acrylonitrile, aniline, carbon tetrachloride, ethylene dibromide, 
formaldehyde, methylene chloride, o-dichlorobenzene, 
octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane, 
p-
dichlorobenzene, perchloroethylene, tris(2-chloroethyl) phosphate, and vinyl chloride. 
The warning sign required by §1910.1024(m)(2) reads: 
DANGER 
REGULATED AREA 
BERYLLIUM 
MAY CAUSE CANCER 
CAUSES DAMAGE TO LUNGS 
AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY 
WEAR RESPIRATORY PROTECTION AND PERSONAL PROTECTIVE CLOTHING AND 
EQUIPMENT IN THIS AREA 
In order that it be legible, a sign containing this language would have to be at least the size of a 
3” x 5” index card. The foreseeable laboratory above could be required to post 345 sq. in. of 

signage containing nearly 600 words. It is not difficult to envision that chemical-intensive 
laboratories would eventually be physically unable to comply with all required postings as they 
would occupy a space larger than the area of the door. 
EPA should adopt a Laboratory Standard under TSCA that requires development of a 
single, holistic Workplace Chemical Protection Plan rather than require development of a 
multitude of distinct chemical-specific Workplace Chemical Protection Plans. This should 
include unified requirements for laboratory signage with sufficient flexibility to 
accommodate requirements imposed by other regulatory frameworks (e.g. OSHA, NFPA). 
The proposed rule for NMP is poorly tailored to laboratory use and creates an excessive 
regulatory burden. I urge the EPA to align its requirements more closely with OSHA’s Laboratory 
Standard and develop a common approach to chemical regulation that applies to all laboratory 
chemicals. This will ensure effective protection without imposing unnecessary burdens on 
laboratories. 
Thank you for your consideration.

(29 CFR 1910.1200). Companies can consult with an SDS authoring company regarding hazard 
profile of a product to generate an OSHA-compliant SDS.  
 
Here, EPA is requiring a bespoke label statement, by product type. Since these label statements 
fall outside of the standard OSHA HazCom, SDS authoring companies must develop specialized 
algorithms for specific products. This is a costly undertaking. ACA is currently gathering 
additional cost estimates. We hope to provide EPA with additional information.  
 
VI. 
EPA should not require the same detailed warning statement in two SDS Sections. 
EPA proposes adding a lengthy paragraph identifying restrictions by product type in both 
Section 1(c) and Section 15 of the SDS. Providing detailed information in Section 1(c) is 
unnecessarily duplicative and places undue emphasis on NMP, detracting from important use 
information. Section 1 of the SDS is designed so workers can quickly understand chemical 
identity and use, while consulting other sections as needed. EPA’s proposed paragraph will 
likely be the most prominent information in Section 1, due to the size of the paragraph. This 
information is better suited for Section 15, instead of Section 1. At a minimum, EPA should draft 
an abbreviated, one sentence statement appropriate for Section 1. For example, Section 1 can 
contain the statement, “This product contains NMP, and it cannot be processed with a 
concentration above 0.1% by weight in certain products.”    
VII. 
ACA supports a de minimis threshold of 0.1%, while noting a regulatory and 
scientific basis for a higher threshold. 
ACA supports EPA’s proposal for a de minimis threshold of 0.1% while also requesting that EPA 
raise the threshold to align with OSHA Hazard Communication requirements at 1%. Raising the 
threshold would assist with compliance throughout the value chain, since systems are already 
in place that identify NMP in products and readily communicate information. Raising the 
threshold is also supported by EPA’s risk evaluation. In arriving at a 0.1% threshold, EPA relies 
on over-estimated risk through an inappropriate surrogate exposure pathway. Since 0.1% is 
based on an over-estimate, EPA can feasibly raise the de minimis to 1% without compromising 
exposure protections, especially considering the regulatory benefits of a 1% threshold aligned 
with OSHA hazard communication requirements. 
In the 2020 Risk Evaluation for NMP EPA concludes “an NMP concentration of 0.1% would 
achieve exposure concentrations that do not contribute to unreasonable risk up to an air 

8 
concentration of 30 mg/m3.”6 Yet, the unreasonable risk finding is driven by concerns for 
dermal exposure, not inhalation.7 
ACA is also concerned that EPA’s air modeling methods assume 8 hours of dermal exposure, 
with no PPE.8 As noted by ACA members, this would only occur if workers consistently handled 
NMP by completely ignoring all current safety requirements. This is impossible due to 
workplace practices. The inaccuracy of relying on EPA air modeling is compounded by risk being 
based on dermal exposure, not inhalation.  
Assuming risk driven by dermal exposure, the corresponding chronic exposure air concentration 
value should be 0% on EPA’s NMP Air Concentration and Weight Fraction Modeling Table. In 
the zero column for air concentration, the MOE is above the benchmark MOE of 30 at a weight 
fraction of 2.2%, over 20 times higher than the proposed 0.1% threshold. Considering this, a 
0.1% threshold assumes extremely high NMP concentrations in air. This is unrealistic since NMP 
is not volatile. EPA notes low volatility when concluding unreasonable risk is driven by dermal 
exposure. EPA’s risk estimate allows for a 1% threshold with no unreasonable risk. 
VIII. 
Compliance schedule is not feasible. 
EPA is proposing a very short compliance time frame with bans on import, labeling 
requirements and container size restrictions taking effect within a year of the effective date, 
with all other requirements phased in within two years. The time frame is not realistic, 
especially considering that products do not have an imminent or acute risk, requiring 
immediate removal from the market. Reformulation of coatings products, under a best case 
scenario, would take 2-3 years, assuming an alternative is available. Products must be tested for 
performance characteristics and hazard minimization. Since coatings products perform an 
important sustainability function by protecting substrates, efficacy testing is critical when 
reformulating. ACA recommends extending all compliance dates by at least two years, but 
preferably longer. 
ACA further recommends unlimited sell-through for products placed on the market prior to the 
compliance date, especially for the container size, label and SDS requirements. An unlimited 
sell-through is required so products manufactured prior to the compliance date can clear the 
market. Many regulations take this approach. For example, California Air Resources Board’s 
consumer product regulations allow unlimited sell through to accommodate formulation 
changes and changes to labeling and container size. Without unlimited sell through, EPA by

IX. 
Conclusion 
 
ACA appreciates the opportunity to comment. As described above, ACA provides the following 
suggestions: 
• EPA should not pre-determine which industry sectors can comply with EPA’s proposed 
risk mitigation strategy to impose bans.  
• EPA should allow cleaning and degreasing operations at coatings facilities in compliance 
with the WCPP. 
• EPA should not restrict coatings additives, used as a raw material, to a 45% 
concentration limit. 
• EPA should align its reference to “automotive care” products with the CDR, referencing 
“automotive cleaners” and “automotive seem sealers,” while distinguishing automotive 
cleaning products from paint removal products. 
• EPA should clarify that “coatings” are not included under the CoU for metal products 
not covered elsewhere. 
• EPA should not finalize the container size limit for consumer products. In the alternative, 
the requirement should only apply to regulated products when manufactured above the 
concentration limits imposed on their industrial or commercial counterparts. 
• EPA should considerably shorten the consumer product label statements considering 
limited space availability due to required text on paint container labels and/or provide a 
website with additional information. 
• EPA must more realistically factor costs of SDS updates into its analysis. 
• EPA should modify the proposed label statement in SDS Section 1 so it concisely conveys 
information without replicating the full paragraph as proposed. 
• EPA should raise the de minimis to 1% or alternatively adopt the 0.1% threshold. 
• EPA should extend all compliance dates by at least two years, with an unlimited sell 
through for products manufactured, labeled and packaged prior to the compliance

AFL-CIO Comments on EPA’s Proposed Rule on n-Methylpyrrolidone (NMP); Regulation 
Under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA)  
EPA-HQ-OPPT-2020-0744-0015 
July 29, 2024 
 
 
The AFL-CIO welcomes this opportunity to comment on EPA’s proposed risk 
management rule for n-Methylpyrrolidone (NMP). The AFL-CIO is the federation of 60 national 
and international labor unions representing 12.5 million working people across a wide variety of 
industries. Our unions represent workers in a broad range of industries where they are exposed to 
NMP, including construction; manufacturing of electronic parts, semiconductors, machinery, 
appliances, and lithium batteries; the petrochemical industry; and an array of other industries in 
which they regularly use and are exposed to products that contain NMP. The AFL-CIO and its 
affiliated unions therefore have a vital interest in the elimination of the unreasonable risks posed 
by workplace exposure to NMP and support EPA finalizing this risk management rule, with 
changes. 
 
I. 
The Proposed WCPP Appropriately Incorporates the Hierarchy of Controls for 
Dermal Exposures 
 
 
We strongly support EPA’s proposed worker chemical protection plan (WCPP), requiring 
owners and operators to implement the hierarchy of controls to reduce dermal contact to NMP. 
As EPA explained in the preamble to the proposed rule, addressing workplace exposures through 
the hierarchy of controls is considered best practice by the industrial hygiene community. This 
strategy prioritizes “exposure control strategies from most preferred to least preferred 
techniques,” starting with elimination of the hazard as most favored, followed by substitution 

2 
 
with a less hazardous substance, engineering controls, administrative controls, and “finally, use 
of PPE.”1  
 
We also strongly support the importance that EPA has placed on access for affected 
workers and their “designated representatives” to the exposure control plan, which is also 
consistent with other occupational health standards. Where a union represents the workers 
exposed to NMP, it is entirely appropriate that they have access to the control plan, since worker 
health and safety is a mandatory subject of collective bargaining under the National Labor 
Relations Act, and access to information on hazards and their control is a key means of 
effectively bargaining on behalf of exposed workers. We urge EPA, however, to also require 
owners and operators to consult with their workers and their representatives in developing their 
exposure control plans. Workers often have significant insights into how employers can 
effectively control chemical exposures, and securing their buy-in for mitigation strategies is key 
to their successful implementation.  
 
II. 
The Proposed Prescriptive Controls for Workers Facing Unreasonable 
Inhalation Risks are Inadequate, and Must Instead Follow the Hierarchy of 
Controls 
   
 
While we believe the WCPP establishes an effective means of controlling workplace 
exposures, the proposal for prescriptive controls falls short. EPA has identified certain conditions 
of use in which the levels of air concentration contribute to NMP’s unreasonable risk, and 
therefore addressing dermal exposures alone “is not expected to address the unreasonable risk.”2 
Yet, even though EPA has explained that under the hierarchy of controls, “the use of respirators

and dermal PPE should only be considered after all other steps have been taken to reduce 
exposures,”3 the proposed prescriptive controls direct owners and operators to use dermal PPE 
and respirators, without first determining whether they can eliminate or minimize exposures by 
implementing more effective control strategies. This is not only inconsistent with EPA’s 
acknowledgment, in the preamble to this rule, of the importance of following the hierarchy of 
controls--and not relying primarily on PPE—it is at odds with the approach EPA has taken in 
proposing and finalizing its other risk management rules. EPA has given no reasons for departing 
from that precedent here. 
 
We urge EPA to revise the prescriptive control requirements in proposed Section 751.211 
in several respects. First, having already determined that inhalation exposures contribute to 
unreasonable risks in these identified conditions of use, EPA should set an existing chemical 
exposure limit (ECEL). Without an ECEL, owners and operators will have no benchmark against 
which to determine whether they are adequately controlling inhalation exposures and, if 
respiratory protection is necessary, no basis for selecting the appropriate level of protection. 
Second, EPA should require monitoring, to determine whether workplace exposures exceed the 
ECEL in the first instance, and whether the controls owners/operators implement are effective. 
Third, EPA should require owners and operators to follow the hierarchy of controls in addressing 
both inhalation and dermal exposures. Fourth, given EPA’s finding that, as a general matter, 
dermal exposures are the primary driver of the unreasonable risk NMP poses, EPA must make 
clear that owners and operators engaged in the conditions of use listed in proposed Section 
751.211 remain obligated to address dermal exposures, even if monitoring shows that inhalation 
exposures are below the ECEL.

When the Occupational Safety and Health Administration issued its methylene chloride 
standard in 1997, many employers substituted NMP, since it was unregulated. EPA now 
regulates methylene chloride under TSCA, requiring owners and operators to install engineering 
controls and otherwise follow the hierarchy of controls in those conditions of use in which 
methylene chloride is still permitted. Setting such weak prescriptive controls for the conditions 
of use where workers face inhalation risks from NMP exposure will only create incentives for 
more owners and operators to substitute NMP for methylene chloride.    
 
In short, the requirements for the conditions of use listed in Section 751.211 must be 
strengthened. They should more closely mirror the WCPP’s requirements in Section 751.209 for 
following the hierarchy of controls, developing an exposure control plan, designating restricted 
areas, and providing training and access to information. In addition to those requirements, 
however, EPA should establish an ECEL and monitoring requirements for these conditions of 
use. 
 
III. 
EPA’s Data Show Lithium-Ion Battery Manufacturing and Additional 
Conditions of Use Pose Inhalation Risks 
 
 
EPA has designated certain conditions of use for which it has concluded dermal controls 
are sufficient (those subject to a WCPP) and others for which both dermal and inhalation 
controls are necessary (those subject to the prescriptive controls). Its own data, however, show 
that in addition to the conditions of use listed in Section 751.211, there are other categories in 
which inhalation contributes significantly to the risk.  
EPA has determined that a margin of exposure (MOE) of less than 30 between the point 
of departure and the modeled exposure represents an unreasonable risk.4 For some of the life

cycle categories EPA evaluated, the MOEs and the high exposures the agency reported in its 
NMP Supplemental File support the conclusion that inhalation exposure is an important driver of 
unreasonable risk.5 Lithium-ion battery manufacturing is an example where EPA’s data, along 
with other evidence, clearly show that high inhalation exposures compel more robust worker 
protections. 
EPA’s data on lithium-ion cell manufacturing shows 8 chronic male worker scenarios in 
which the MOE is less than 30 and the 8-hour TWA exceeds 7 mg/m3. Four of these are cathode 
coating scenarios in which the 8-hour TWA is 39.7 mg/m3. There is also one acute female

Coalition advised EPA that this work is “frequently” performed in closed systems involving no

unreasonable risks from inhalation exposures.  
This is but one example of how important it is for EPA to stop relying on assertions by 
any industry alone—without confirmation through independent site visits and testing and worker 
verifications—to determine the specific risk management practices needed through regulation. In 
any industry, there will always be better and worse actors. Not only do the employees of the 
worse actors need to be protected by regulation, but regulation plays an important role in leveling 
the playing field so the better actors are protected from unfair competition from actors who do 
not invest in worker and environmental protections. In addition, the fact that members of an

Contrary to EPA’s assumption, some occupational non-users (ONUs) such as 
maintenance and skilled trades workers, by the nature of their jobs, are often required to 
open and/or enter closed systems and either routinely or from time-to-time, may have acute 
exposures that are much higher than production workers. Nowhere does EPA account for 
these workers who may have no exposure on many days, but on some days have to open

V. 
Requests for Modifying the Training Specifications in the Proposed Rule  
The proposed rule’s training requirements should align with existing OSHA Hazardous 
Communication (“HazCom”) standard chemical safety training requirements in 21 C.F.R. § 
1910.1200(h)(1), the training in other OSHA chemical specific standards, and OSHA’s PPE selection and 
training rules and guidances.   
Under HazCom, employers must already provide employees with effective information and 
training on hazardous chemicals in their work area at the time of their initial assignment, and whenever 
a new chemical hazard the employees have not previously been trained about is introduced into their 
work area.  Note that OSHA allows information and training that is designed to cover categories of hazards 
(e.g., flammability, carcinogenicity) or specific chemicals.  Chemical-specific information must always be 
available through labels and safety data sheets.  Furthermore, § 1910.1200(b)(1) specifies that all 
employers must “provide information to their employees about the hazardous chemicals to which they 
are exposed, by means of a hazard communication program, labels and other forms of warning, safety 
data sheets, and information and training . . .”  In § 1910.1200(b)(4)(iii), employers are specifically directed 
to provide information and training to employees “to the extent necessary to protect them in the event 
of a spill or leak of a hazardous chemical from a sealed container.”   
The HazCom standard specifies in § 1910.1200(e)(1) that employers shall develop, implement, 
and maintain at each workplace, a written hazard communication program that describes how employee 
information and training will be met, a list of the hazardous chemicals known to be present, and the 
methods the employer will use to inform employees of the hazards of non-routine tasks (e.g., cleaning of 
reactor vessels).   
There is no annual training requirement for general HazCom.  In § 1910.1200(h)(1), OSHA specifies 
that “employers shall provide employees with effective information and training on hazardous chemicals 
in their work area at the time of their initial assignment, and whenever a new chemical hazard the 
employees have not previously been trained about is introduced into their work area.”  Neither is there a 
general training requirement in OSHA’s general PPE standard.  Some, but not all OSHA standards for 
specific chemicals call for annual training or retraining.    
In contrast, this proposed rule has two separate training sections that require annual training, one 
for PPE and one on this rule.  The proposed rule specifies in (e)(4) that employees must be trained in PPE 
1) annually; or 2) whenever the owner or operator has reason to believe that a previously trained person 
does not have the required understanding and skill to properly use PPE; or 3) when changes in the 
workplace or in PPE to be used render the previous training obsolete.  The proposed rule in (f)(4) and (5) 
requires training on the requirements of this rule 1) prior to or at the time of initial assignment to a job

involving potential exposure to NMP; 2) retraining annually; 3) updated training whenever there are 
workplace changes, such as modifications of tasks or procedures or the institution of new tasks or

While measurement-based methods such as charcoal patches show promise for in-field dermal

internal exposure, such as biomonitoring of blood or urine, and inhalation exposure measurements.

Uncertainties are already incorporated into risk management programs to assure that risk

a given task.  To understand the risk for dermal exposure to chemicals, an OEHS professional qualitatively 
observes whether there is potential for skin contact with an agent of concern and semi-quantitatively (i.e., 
through modeling) or quantitatively (i.e., through sample collection) assesses potential exposures to allow 
for identification and prioritization of tasks requiring control measures.  For example, as dermal protection 
strategies often rely on an individual worker’s hygiene practices, worker behavior is monitored as an 
important determinant in the dermal exposure pathway.18   
In quantitative sampling, there are additional uncertainties associated with the use of charcoal 
cloths, pads, or patches as a sampling substrate in interception, surrogate, or dosimeter techniques to 
estimate skin contamination or exposure potential.19  Empirical measurement of dermal exposure can be 
challenging due to the sporadic nature of skin exposure, uncertainties regarding skin absorption, lack of 
retention on or recovery of analyte from sampled skin or surfaces, a lack of relevant sampling methods, 
and a lack of occupational exposure limits with which to compare sampling results.  Methods to sample 
and evaluate dermal exposure to chemicals include removal of the agent from the skin or work surface 
(i.e., wipe samples), interception of the agent on substrates prior to skin contact (i.e., charcoal pad 
testing), or in situ techniques (i.e., use of fluorescent tracers).20  This type of sampling assumes that 
substrate collection and retention occur similarly to that of skin; however, effective use of interception 
methods such as charcoal pad testing is highly dependent on variability in contaminant deposition rates, 
clothing type, anatomical characteristics and duration of skin contact, and chemical retention and

Executive Summary 
The Fertilizer Institute (TFI), representing the nation's fertilizer industry, submits these comments 
in response to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) proposed regulation of N-
Methylpyrrolidone (NMP) under the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) (Docket No. EPA-HQ-
OPPT-2020-0744). Published on June 14, 2024, the proposed rule suggests a complete prohibition 
on the industrial and commercial use of NMP in fertilizer and other agricultural chemical 
manufacturing processes. 
 
TFI's member companies are integral to the entire fertilizer supply chain, essential for feeding a 
global population projected to exceed 9.5 billion by 2050. Fertilizers, made possible by TFI's 
members, enable the growth of half of the world's food supply. Urease inhibitors, containing NMP, 
play a critical role in enhancing the efficiency of fertilizers, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, 
and minimizing nutrient loss. 
 
Urease inhibitors are a type of Enhanced Efficiency Fertilizer (EEF) that prevent the rapid 
transformation of nitrogen into forms that can be lost to the environment. These inhibitors are 
crucial for sustainable agriculture, helping maximize crop nutrient use while minimizing 
environmental impact. They function by inhibiting the enzyme urease, which breaks down urea 
into ammonia, thereby reducing ammonia volatilization and ensuring more nitrogen is available 
for plant uptake. 
 
The EPA's proposed rule aims to ban the use of NMP in fertilizers, citing concerns about dermal 
exposure risks. However, EPA’s ban seems to be primarily based on a lack of knowledge about 
agricultural uses of NMP and the robust workplace safety protections and practices of facilities 
producing and handling agricultural chemicals. TFI supports the alternative approach proposed for 
fertilizer and agricultural chemicals of a Worker Chemical Protection Program (WCPP), which 
includes strict safety protocols to prevent dermal contact with NMP. The proposed ban disregards 
the existing safety measures and engineering controls in place that already minimize exposure risks 
effectively. 
 
TFI members adhere to stringent safety and environmental standards, including the use of personal 
protective equipment (PPE), hazard communication, and training programs in compliance with 
OSHA regulations. The industry has robust procedures for handling and applying urease inhibitors, 
ensuring minimal exposure to NMP. Engineering controls, such as enclosed blending systems and 
automated dosing, further reduce the risk of dermal contact. 
 
TFI urges the EPA to reconsider its proposed ban and adopt the WCPP alternative, which balances 
safety, environmental protection, and economic considerations. The agricultural sector is 
committed to sustainable practices and compliance with federal regulations, as exemplified by 
initiatives like the ResponsibleAg program. A collaborative regulatory approach is essential to 
maintaining agricultural productivity and environmental stewardship.

II. 
Background on Urease Inhibitors  
 
A. 
The Function and Purpose of Urease Inhibitors 
 
EEF is a term defined by the Association of American Plant Food Control Officials (“AAPFCO”) 
as a “fertilizer product with characteristics that allow increased nutrient availability and reduces 
potential of nutrient loss to the environment e.g. gaseous losses, leaching, or runoff.”4 EEFs 
include a broad range of products that vary in modes of action, but all slow the transformation of 
nitrogen to forms that are easily lost to the environment. Not only does this help to reduce nitrogen 
(N) losses that are detrimental to our air and water, but also help to maximize crop use of the 
nutrient. Therefore, from both a nutrient management and environmental stewardship perspective, 
the utilization of EEF products is essential for sustainable agricultural practices. Use of EEFs is 
well established as a conservation practice that can be easily implemented by growers5. EEFs do 
not require farmers to change their nitrogen programs, sources, or application methods. EEFs are 
formulated to be applied with many sources of N fertilizer and do not require additional or 
specialized equipment for application. EEFs remain a breakthrough innovation for reducing 
nutrient pollution that is easily accessible for all farmers. Few conservation practices exist that do 
not require major changes in farming practices, and thus EEFs remain one of the most important 
conservation technologies in the world.  
 
Urease inhibitors, a category of EEFs, are chemical substances designed to prevent the activity of 
the urease enzyme.6 Urease is a ubiquitous enzyme and is widespread in soils and plant residues. 
This enzyme, in the presence of water, breaks down (or hydrolyzes) urea into ammonia. In soils 
with high pH or in environments where the soil and residue do not adequately buffer against pH 
increases, the swift hydrolysis of urea can lead to an accumulation of ammonia (NH3) instead of 
ammonium (NH4). With higher soil pH, there are less H ions present, thus more ammonia (NH3) 
forms versus the plant available ammonium (NH4). This ammonia is a greenhouse gas (GHG) that 
can escape into the atmosphere and can contribute significant N losses in some circumstances. In 
extreme cases, research has shown that over 50% of an applied nitrogen fertilizer can be lost as 
ammonia.

By inhibiting the hydrolysis of urea, urease inhibitors help prevent ammonia volatilization, thereby 
keeping the nitrogen in the fertilizer in its urea form. Because urea is highly soluble in water, this 
inhibition provides time for rainfall or irrigation to move the urea into the soil. Once the urea is 
incorporated into the soil, even to a shallow depth of 2-3 inches, it is protected from ammonia 
volatilization. This is because the ammonium (NH4) is quickly absorbed onto soil cation exchange 
sites.  
 
To manufacture urease inhibitors, solvents such as NMP are needed. Solvents that stabilize the 
active ingredient in urease inhibitors are essential for successful product formulation. These 
inhibitors are typically mixed with fertilizers, whether liquid or dry, in small quantities as part of 
the final nutrient product. Urease inhibitor solutions are blended with urea or liquid urea 
ammonium nitrate (“UAN”) at fertilizer distribution or agricultural retail facilities (hereinafter, 
blending facilities) by trained operators with specialized blending equipment.7  
 
Urease inhibitors are often combined with nitrification inhibitors and called dual inhibitors. In 
addition to slowing hydrolysis of urea, these dual inhibitors also slow nitrification through the 
nitrification inhibitor properties. Researchers have explained the use of these dual inhibitors 
“…enables producers to balance crop production and environmental conservation goals without 
pollution tradeoffs.”  
 
Urease inhibitors provide substantial environment benefits. Studies in the great plains found urease 
inhibitors reduce ammonia losses by 66% and protect nitrogen from volatilization for 2 to 3 weeks 
in acidic soils and more than 7 weeks in alkaline soils.8 In a recent meta-analysis on inhibitors, 
researchers found that across 182 studies urease inhibitors enhanced crop yields by 5%, and 
reduced NH3 volatilization by 51%.9 Urease inhibitors play a major role in protecting N from loss 
in agricultural soils and are a vital tool for growers.

B. 
Formulation of Urease Inhibitors 
 
NMP is used as a solvent in the formulation of urease inhibitors. NMP is added to a mix tank along 
with other co-solvents, dyes, and the active ingredient, NBPT. Production takes place at custom 
manufacturing facilities where operators receive training on the chemical hazards of the materials 
they handle, as well as the proper use of personal protective equipment (“PPE”) for agricultural 
chemicals.11 
 
i. Formulation Process 
 
Urease inhibitors are formulated in batch-mixing processes. To formulate urease inhibitors, raw 
materials are loaded through the top of mixing tanks. NMP is pumped from bulk storage or 275-
gallon totes through flexible transfer lines into a mixing tank. Raw materials are then pumped into 
the mixing tank through flexible transfer lines. Induction12 or mixing tanks with a manway cover13 
may be used. Once all raw materials are loaded into the mixing tank, the system is closed and the 
solution is mixed with an automated system. It takes approximately 60 minutes to create a 
homogenous solution. Once the formulation is complete, the finished product is then pumped 
through flexible transfer lines from the mix tank into 275-gallon totes or 2.5-gallon packaging 
containers. Mixing equipment and procedures are designed minimize the duration and frequency 
of worker exposure to raw materials being handled.

Regular maintenance and cleaning of formulation equipment include, clean out of tanks and

iii. Existing Protections and Workplace Safety Practices 
 
Worker activities that present potential points of dermal contact with NMP solutions in the 
formulation of urease inhibitors include the loading of the mix tank and the unloading of the 
finished product into final containers. Urease inhibitor formulation processes are physically 
designed (e.g. pumping mechanisms to load and unload materials, automated mixing, and enclosed 
mixing tanks) to avoid dermal contact when operated properly. Based on consultation with industry 
experts, batch formulation of urease inhibitors is estimated to occur 60 production days per year. 
Loading the mixing tanks to formulate a batch of urease inhibitors is estimated to on average take 
30 minutes. Unloading of finished product into final containers takes approximately 1.5 hours. 
During the formulation of a batch of urease inhibitors, workers perform activities that present 
potentially exposure to NMP for a total duration of 2 hours per production day. 
 
Manufacturing facilities comply with OSHA standards, which mandate hazard communication 
training, PPE training, and the implementation of appropriate risk management practices as 
indicated by raw material and finished product labels and Safety Data Sheets (“SDS”). Training

Application of Urease Inhibitors to Fertilizer Products  
Urease inhibitors are applied at distribution and retail locations where bulk fertilizer is sold. 
Distributors and retailers treat urea or urea-ammonium nitrate (“UAN”) solutions with urease 
inhibitors before loading trucks with the treated products. Urease inhibitors typically contain 15-

accomplished with liquid dosing systems.

ii. Maintenance and Cleaning Activities  
 
Maintenance and cleaning of blending equipment occurs when there is significant dust build-up 
within the system. Cleaning activities involve pressure washing blending equipment from above, 
eliminating the need for workers to physically enter the blending equipment. During the cleaning 
process, concentration of NMP encountered by workers is below that in final treated fertilizer

as detailed further in Section II.C.iv. of TFI’s comments. 
 
Maintenance activities that present a potential point of dermal contact with NMP-containing urease 
inhibitors is limited to the replacement of liquid dosing system nozzles. Nozzle replacement is 
infrequent, only occurring as needed and typically not more than once a year. Workers performing 
this maintenance wear appropriate PPE as detailed further in Section II.C.iv. of TFI’s comments. 
 
iii. Seasonality of Bending Operations 
 
Agricultural retail and blending operations are inherently seasonal businesses since nutrient 
application closely coincides with crop needs to reduce losses to the environment. In row crop 
agriculture nitrogen fertilizer is typically applied once or twice per growing season, with urease 
inhibitors used only in early spring or late fall. Therefore, workers at agriculture retail facilities 
handle urease inhibitor products for only six to eight weeks per year. Similarly, distributors or 
wholesalers that treat fertilizer sold to retail locations typically treat products for only two to four 
months of the year. At distribution/wholesale facilities, worker activities, protections, and potential

iv. Existing Protections and Workplace Safety Practices   
 
The chance of dermal contact with urease inhibitors is minimal during fertilizer blending.

Fertilizer Exceeds the Agency’s Statutory Authority 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Once EPA determines that the manufacture, processing, distribution in commerce, use, or 
disposal of a chemical substance presents an “unreasonable risk,” TSCA § 6(a)19 mandates 
that the Agency issue a risk management rule so the substance no longer presents such a risk. 
However, Congress did not provide EPA with unfettered discretion in promulgating such 
rules. Rather, Congress mandated that the Agency’s risk management rule only addresses the 
unreasonable risk “to the extent necessary” to do so.20 Under this standard, if any other 
measure would address the identified risks then a ban is impermissible because fully banning 
use would go beyond “the extent necessary.”

proposes a worker chemical protection program (“WCPP”).22 EPA’s disparate treatment of 
the fertilizer/agricultural chemicals COU, when compared to the other industrial/commercial 
COUs eligible for a WCPP, is based on the Agency’s “uncertainty relative to the feasibility 
of exposure reduction to sufficiently address the unreasonable risk across the broad range of 
work environments and activities.”23  As an initial matter, lack of information is an

In certain particular applications, it is necessary to distribute the active ingredient (NBPT) using a 
minimum amount of solvent when applied to one ton of urea. The target concentration of NBPT 
to be applied to urea is 600-900 ppm NPBT. To successfully achieve this objective, NBPT needs 
to be very soluble in the solvent system (25%-35% NBPT) and the solvent system needs to be 
effective at coating urea when as little as 1.5 quarts of product is applied to one-ton of urea. 
 
Information on application types and processes for urease inhibitors is provided in Section II of 
TFI’s comments. As noted, urease inhibitor products containing NMP can be applied to urea (solid 
fertilizer pellets) or UAN (liquid fertilizer solutions). There is no aerosol application of urease 
inhibitors to fertilizer products when treating urea or UAN.

because another option exists.  Rather, EPA’s authority under TSCA §6 remains bound by the 
seminal statutory instruction that it is limited to imposing controls “to the extent necessary” to 
mitigate risk.  Where other less invasive alternatives exist (as here), the mere existence of an

The Association of Equipment Manufacturers (AEM) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed rule, n-Methylpyrrolidone (NMP); Regulation Under the 
Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA)1 hereafter referred to as the Proposed Rule. We look forward to 
sharing the expertise and technical knowledge of our industry sectors. We believe it is critically important 
when developing regulations, that the interest of all stakeholders be considered and understood. 
 
AEM is the North American-based international trade group representing off-road equipment manufacturers 
and suppliers with more than 1,000 member companies and over 200 product lines in the construction, 
agriculture, mining, forestry, and utility industries. The equipment manufacturing industry in the United States 
supports 2.8 million jobs and contributes roughly $288 billion to the economy every year. Our industries 
remain a critical part of the U.S. economy and represent 12 percent of all manufacturing jobs in the United 
States. Our members develop and produce a multitude of technologies in a wide range of products, 
components, and systems that ensure off-road equipment remains safe and efficient, while at the same time 
reducing carbon emissions and environmental hazards.  Finished products have a life cycle measured in 
decades and are designed for professional recycling of the entire product at the end of life.  Additionally, our 
industry sectors strive to develop climate friendly propulsion systems and support robust environmental 
stewardship programs around the world. 
 
The off-road equipment manufacturing industry understands the value and importance of using sound 
science to inform future policymaking decisions. AEM strives to be a key stakeholder in these policymaking 
discussions. To ensure that new rules meet their objectives with accurate and complete data, AEM wants to 
support EPA’s approach as well as make a request that EPA take into consideration the following points: 
 
1. AEM supports the EPA’s proposed de minimis of .1%, but requests clarification on the applicability of 
this provision to complex articles and finished goods.  
2. AEM supports EPA’s regulatory approach which takes into consideration the conditions of use and 
the risks associated with end uses.  
3. AEM asks EPA to clarify the specific use case: Processing of NMP for incorporation into articles in 
lubricants and as a lubricant additive in machinery manufacturing.  
4. AEM asks EPA to clarify their stance on transition periods and exemptions for replacement parts. 
 
AEM supports EPA’s proposed de minimis levels:

In the Proposed Rule, EPA introduced a de minims level of .1% for products containing NMP to account for 
impurities that do not contribute to the unreasonable risks associated with NMP. AEM supports this approach 
to mitigating the risks associated with hazardous chemicals. 
 
One of the larger challenges of designing out substances of concern is identifying where these substances 
are found in our products. Historically, the off-road equipment industry has had very little expertise regarding 
the collection and storage of data for chemical management regulations. This educational issue, endemic 
throughout the supply chain, is compounded by the wider compliance environment many of these companies 
operate in. Smaller manufacturers of components often do not store chemicals above the reporting 
thresholds required under US law (e.g. CDR, SARA 313 reporting rules). As a result, many companies in our 
supply chains never cultivated the systems or expertise needed to gather and store the relevant chemical 
data for the components and parts they manufacture and distribute.  
 
The task is made more difficult due to the confidential business information (CBI) protections many bulk 
chemical manufacturers utilize to conceal the composition of their products, making downstream reporting 
extremely challenging to accomplish. Additionally, International suppliers follow various global regulations 
which differ from each other, deepening the data collection obstacles faced by the global supply chain. 
 
Furthermore, without a de minimis threshold manufacturers will need to account for, and remove, trace 
amounts of chemicals of concern in their products, which will require expensive lab testing to confirm. 
Companies manufacturing and selling complex products with hundreds of thousands of parts, need to rely on 
supplier reporting and data collection to understand where their risks lie. Establishing de minimis thresholds, 
addressing CBI concerns, and distinguishing between intentionally added chemicals and unintentional 
impurities, simplifies this task and make the likelihood of compliance and success much higher. 
 
For all these reasons listed, AEM supports the EPA’s introduction of a de minimis threshold standard in this 
rule.   
 
Clarification on applicability of the de minimis standard: 
 
While AEM supports the use of de minimis standards in these rulemakings, we do have a question on what 
this threshold standard applies to.  
 
In the recent publication of the EPA’s Methylene Chloride; Regulation Under the Toxic Substances Control 
Act (TSCA)2, the rule introduced a de minimis threshold in Part 751 Subpart B § 751.101(b). This section 
states that:  
 
Unless otherwise specified in this subpart, the prohibitions and restrictions of this subpart 
to not apply to products containing methylene chloride at thresholds less than .1 percent 
by weight.3 
 
In 40 CFR Part 751 Subpart A § 751.5, the definition of products is as follows: 
 
means the chemical substance, a mixture containing the chemical substance, or any object that 
contains the chemical substance or mixture containing the chemical substance that is not an article.4 
 
Based on the definitions found in 751.5, the de minimis threshold would not apply to articles, only to 
products. This would create an immediate compliance issue for manufacturers, as articles are comprised of 
chemicals and mixtures or products, as they are currently defined in this definitions section of the CFR. 
Under this scenario, any product which contains a regulated substance under the de minimis threshold would 
immediately make the article it is incorporated in non-compliant with the rule.

Request:  
 
AEM requests clarification from EPA on this specific issue, specifically with regards to how it relates to the 
NMP proposed rule, as well as future TSCA risk management rules. If AEM’s understanding is correct, we 
request that EPA ensure future rules ensure that regulated entities have a viable compliance pathway for 
their products. 
 
AEM supports the EPS’s regulatory approach: 
 
Certain chemicals can provide a great societal benefit, with low environmental and human health risks based 
on the manufacturing process and end-use applications. Due to the fact that many chemicals, such as NMP, 
are used in a wide range of applications with various risks associated with their intended use. These end use 
applications require further assessment and consideration by policymakers to determine their true hazard 
profile.  
 
EPA’s regulatory approach throughout their proposed rule prioritizes occupational risks, conditions of use, 
engineering controls, PPE use, and other measures to mitigate the identified risks with NMP. This approach 
recognizes the valuable uses of NMP for society and avoids broad prohibitions on the substance across the 
US market. AEM supports this approach in this rule, as well as others that may come in the future.  
 
 
Clarification on Definition: 
 
In the Proposed Rule, EPA states that they are proposing to prohibit the manufacture (including import), 
processing, distribution in commerce, and industrial and commercial use of NMP for five occupational uses. 
One of these uses EPA defines as: 
 
Processing, incorporation into articles in lubricants and lubricant additives in machinery 
manufacturing. This condition of use refers to the process or preparation when NMP is incorporated 
into articles in lubricants and lubricant additives in machinery manufacturing, and metal finishing 
operations conducted as part of machinery manufacturing. Metal finishing is a broad term used in 
industry to include a wide variety of processes that alter the surface of metal substrates, such as 
cleaning, coating, etching, and invasive quality testing. 
 
Request: 
 
AEM would like clarification from EPA regarding this definition. Is this use case only for lubricants used in 
manufacturing environments? When EPA references machinery manufacturing, does this mean machines 
used to manufacture products, or in the manufacturing of machines and machinery products.  
 
Receiving clarification on this definition will help the off-road equipment industry understand the scope and 
intent of this proposed rule moving forward. 
 
 
Off-Road Equipment Replacement Parts Phase-Out Timelines: 
 
Based on the language regarding lubricants and lubricant additives in machinery manufacturing in the 
previous section, AEM is unclear on the scope of products this rule impacts. Depending on this clarification 
from EPA, AEM would like EPA to consider introducing transition times for new equipment and replacement 
parts. 
  
Off-road equipment operates in some of the most demanding and severe environments over a product life 
cycle measured in decades. The equipment are highly complex pieces of machinery requiring each 
manufacturer to undertake component and system level qualifications to ensure the necessary performance 
characteristics are met.

Working under these design requirements AEM member companies estimate that replacing a regulated

the operator, maintenance personnel, the worksite, and the environment.

system redesigns, regulators like EPA, California Air Resource Board (CARB), and the EU Commission
